questions.title: Branch of the second part of the axillary artery
questions.question: One of the following is a branch from the 2nd part of the axillary artery:

explanations.A: Correct. Pectoralis minor crosses the axillary artery and divides it into three parts, each giving a set number of branches (one, two, three): the first part (medial to pectoralis minor) gives the superior thoracic artery; the second part (behind pectoralis minor) gives the thoraco-acromial and lateral thoracic arteries; the third part (lateral to pectoralis minor) gives the subscapular, anterior and posterior circumflex humeral arteries. The lateral thoracic artery, running along serratus anterior, is one of the second part's two branches.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The subscapular artery is one of the three branches of the third part.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The superior thoracic artery is the sole branch of the first part.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The anterior circumflex humeral artery is one of the three branches of the third part.

questions.learning_objective: Name the lateral thoracic artery as a branch of the axillary artery's second part.

questions.title: Muscle forming the medial wall of the axilla
questions.question: Which muscle forms the medial wall of the axilla?

explanations.A: Correct. Serratus anterior, overlying the upper ribs, forms the medial wall of the axilla. The long thoracic nerve runs along this same muscle's superficial surface, which is why both structures are vulnerable together during axillary surgery or a penetrating chest-wall injury. This pairing — medial wall muscle and the nerve that supplies it lying right on its surface — is a frequently tested spatial relation.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Pectoralis major (with pectoralis minor and the clavipectoral fascia) forms the anterior wall, not the medial wall.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Teres major (with latissimus dorsi) forms the posterior wall, not the medial wall.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Subclavius sits above the axilla proper, contributing to the clavipectoral fascia near the apex, not the medial wall.

questions.learning_objective: Name serratus anterior as forming the medial wall of the axilla.

questions.title: Exception among branches of the axillary artery
questions.question: Which of the following arteries is NOT a branch of the axillary artery?

explanations.A: Incorrect (true, not the exception). The thoraco-acromial artery is a branch of the axillary artery's second part.
explanations.B: Incorrect (true, not the exception). The superior thoracic artery is the sole branch of the first part.
explanations.C: Incorrect (true, not the exception). The posterior circumflex humeral artery is one of the third part's three branches.
explanations.D: Correct. The dorsal scapular artery is not one of the axillary artery's six named branches at all — it typically arises directly from the subclavian artery (or occasionally as a continuation of the transverse cervical artery), running to the medial border of the scapula alongside the dorsal scapular nerve. This is why it is the odd one out among the four options, all of which sound like plausible axillary branches by name association with the shoulder region.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the dorsal scapular artery as arising from the subclavian artery, not the axillary artery.

questions.title: Exception among the contents of the axilla
questions.question: The axilla contains all the following EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect (true, not the exception). Axillary fat fills the spaces between the named contents.
explanations.B: Correct. The trunks of the brachial plexus form higher up, in the posterior triangle of the neck, above the clavicle; only the cords (and their branches) of the plexus have formed by the time the neurovascular bundle reaches the axilla. This is a frequently tested distinction — the axilla's contents are always described in terms of the plexus's cords, never its trunks.
explanations.C: Incorrect (true, not the exception). The axillary tail of the breast (of Spence) projects into the axilla's anterior wall region.
explanations.D: Incorrect (true, not the exception). The axillary vein, formed by the basilic vein and the venae comitantes of the brachial artery, runs through the axilla alongside the artery.

questions.learning_objective: Recognise that the axilla contains the cords of the brachial plexus, not its trunks, which have already formed above the clavicle.

questions.title: Medial boundary of the apex of the axilla
questions.question: The medial boundary of the apex of the axilla is formed by:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The acromion process is not one of the apex's three boundaries.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The clavicle's posterior border forms the apex's anterior boundary, not its medial one, and it is the whole posterior border rather than specifically the lateral third.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The surgical neck of the humerus is not related to the axillary apex at all; it is related instead to the axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral artery lower down, at the quadrangular space.
explanations.D: Correct. The apex of the axilla — the cervico-axillary canal through which the neurovascular bundle enters — is bounded by the posterior border of the clavicle (anteriorly), the outer border of the first rib (medially), and the upper border of the scapula (posteriorly). This narrow triangular opening is why axillary vessel and plexus injuries at the apex are functionally equivalent to injuries just below the clavicle.

questions.learning_objective: Name the outer border of the first rib as the medial boundary of the axillary apex.

questions.title: True statement about the axillary artery
questions.question: The axillary artery:

options.B: Is divided into 3 parts by teres major
options.D: Its first part gives the superior thoracic artery

explanations.A: Incorrect. The axillary artery is the direct continuation of the subclavian artery, beginning at the outer border of the first rib, not a branch of the vertebral artery.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Pectoralis minor, not teres major, divides the axillary artery into its three parts.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The third part is the busiest, giving three branches (subscapular, anterior and posterior circumflex humeral).
explanations.D: Correct. The first part of the axillary artery, medial to pectoralis minor, gives a single branch — the superior thoracic artery — supplying the first and second intercostal spaces and part of serratus anterior. This one-branch-per-part-count pattern (1, 2, 3 branches for parts 1, 2, 3) is a standard memory aid for the whole sequence.

questions.learning_objective: State that the axillary artery's first part gives a single branch, the superior thoracic artery.

questions.title: True statement about the axillary artery, second version
questions.question: The axillary artery:

options.A: Becomes the brachial artery at the upper border of teres major
options.B: Gives rise to the thoraco-acromial artery from its 1st part
options.C: Is the continuation of the subclavian artery
options.D: Is divided into 3 parts by teres minor muscle

explanations.A: Incorrect. The axillary artery becomes the brachial artery at the lower border of teres major, not the upper border.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The thoraco-acromial artery arises from the second part, not the first.
explanations.C: Correct. The axillary artery is simply the named continuation of the subclavian artery once it crosses the outer border of the first rib. It continues in turn as the brachial artery at the lower border of teres major, so one continuous vessel carries three names across its course, split by these two landmarks. This naming convention (subclavian, then axillary, then brachial) is standard across the whole upper limb's arterial supply.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Pectoralis minor, not teres minor, divides the axillary artery into its three parts.

questions.learning_objective: State that the axillary artery is the continuation of the subclavian artery.

questions.title: Exception among structures forming the anterior wall of the axilla
questions.question: The anterior wall of the axilla is formed by all of the following EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect (true, not the exception). Pectoralis minor is one of the three named layers of the anterior wall (with pectoralis major and subclavius/clavipectoral fascia).
explanations.B: Correct. Teres major belongs to the posterior wall (with latissimus dorsi and subscapularis), not the anterior wall — grouping it with the wrong pair of muscles is the trap this item sets. Pectoralis major, pectoralis minor, subclavius and the clavipectoral fascia together make up the full anterior wall.
explanations.C: Incorrect (true, not the exception). Subclavius, near the apex, is part of the anterior wall's upper layer.
explanations.D: Incorrect (true, not the exception). The clavipectoral fascia, between subclavius and pectoralis minor, is part of the anterior wall.

questions.learning_objective: Identify teres major as belonging to the posterior, not anterior, wall of the axilla.

questions.title: Artery accompanying the pectoral group of axillary lymph nodes
questions.question: The pectoral group of axillary lymph nodes lies along the:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The superior thoracic artery is not the vessel the pectoral node group follows.
explanations.B: Correct. The pectoral (anterior) group of axillary lymph nodes lies along the lower border of pectoralis minor, following the lateral thoracic artery and vein. This is the node group that drains most of the breast, which is why it is the first echelon removed or sampled in breast cancer surgery (sentinel node biopsy, axillary clearance). It then passes drainage on to the central and apical groups, the last stop before lymph leaves the axilla for the subclavian trunk.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The subscapular artery is followed instead by the posterior (subscapular) group of axillary nodes.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The thoraco-acromial artery is not the vessel the pectoral node group follows.

questions.learning_objective: State that the pectoral group of axillary lymph nodes follows the lateral thoracic artery.

questions.title: Muscles forming the anterior fold of the axilla
questions.question: The anterior fold of the axilla is formed by:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Pectoralis minor lies deep to pectoralis major and does not itself form the palpable anterior fold.
explanations.B: Correct. The anterior axillary fold, the ridge you can grasp between finger and thumb at the front of the armpit, is formed by pectoralis major alone — its lower free border. The posterior fold, by contrast, is formed by latissimus dorsi and teres major together.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Subclavius lies near the apex, well above the level of the folds, and plays no part in forming either fold.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Since only pectoralis major forms the anterior fold, "all of the above" is not correct.

questions.learning_objective: State that pectoralis major alone forms the anterior axillary fold.

questions.title: Orientation of axillary incisions
questions.question: Incisions in the axilla should be:

options.A: Horizontal and nearer to the medial wall
options.B: Horizontal and nearer to the lateral wall
options.C: Vertical and nearer to the medial wall
options.D: Vertical and nearer to the lateral wall

explanations.A: Correct. Axillary incisions are made horizontally, following the natural skin creases, and kept nearer the medial wall to avoid the major neurovascular bundle (axillary artery, vein and the cords of the brachial plexus), which runs closer to the lateral wall along its course from apex to base. A horizontal incision also heals with a less restrictive scar than a vertical one across a mobile joint region.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Placing the incision nearer the lateral wall risks the neurovascular bundle, which runs there.
explanations.C: Incorrect. A vertical incision crosses the skin creases and tends to scar with contracture across this mobile region.
explanations.D: Incorrect. This combines both problems: a vertical incision nearer the vessel-bearing lateral wall.

questions.learning_objective: State that axillary incisions are made horizontally and near the medial wall, away from the neurovascular bundle on the lateral wall.

questions.title: Position of the second part of the axillary artery
questions.question: The 2nd part of the axillary artery lies:

explanations.A: Incorrect. It is the muscle's relation, not its anterior surface, that defines the second part — the artery lies directly behind it.
explanations.B: Correct. By definition, the axillary artery's second part is the segment lying posterior (deep) to pectoralis minor, between the first part (medial to the muscle) and the third part (lateral to it) — this is exactly how the three parts are named and numbered in the first place. This same landmark also defines the first part (medial to pectoralis minor) and the third part (lateral to it), so naming any part of the axillary artery is really just naming its relation to this one muscle.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Teres major does not define any of the axillary artery's three parts; it is the landmark where the axillary artery becomes the brachial artery.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Teres major is not the landmark used to divide the axillary artery into parts.

questions.learning_objective: State that the axillary artery's second part lies posterior to pectoralis minor.

questions.title: Compression site for distal axillary artery bleeding
questions.question: In case of severe bleeding from the distal part of the axillary artery, we compress it against:

options.A: Medial side of the middle of the humerus
options.B: Lateral side of the middle of the humerus

explanations.A: Incorrect. The mid-humeral shaft is not the standard proximal-control point for the axillary artery.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Same reasoning as A — this is not the recognised compression site.
explanations.C: Correct. Because the axilla itself is a deep, mobile, soft-tissue space where direct pressure on the artery is unreliable, standard first-aid teaching compresses the axillary artery proximally, against the outer border of the first rib — the point where it is most superficial and lies against firm bone, at the root of the neck/shoulder junction. Proximal compression here controls bleeding from any point further along the vessel's course, including its distal (third) part.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The artery lies against the outer, not the inner, border of the first rib at this level.

questions.learning_objective: State that proximal control of axillary artery bleeding compresses the vessel against the outer border of the first rib.

questions.title: Lymph node group in the adipose tissue at the base of the axilla
questions.question: Which lymph node group is present in the adipose tissue at the base of the axilla?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The anterior (pectoral) group lies along the lower border of pectoralis minor, not in the base's fat pad.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The posterior (subscapular) group lies along the posterior axillary wall, not the base.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The lateral group lies along the axillary vein's medial side, in the upper axilla, not the base.
explanations.D: Correct. The central group of axillary lymph nodes is embedded in the fat pad at the base (floor) of the axilla, roughly midway between the anterior and posterior folds — it is often the largest, most easily palpable group clinically, and receives drainage from the other three peripheral groups (anterior, posterior, lateral) before passing it on to the apical group. Because it sits at the lowest, most dependent point of the axilla, it is also the group most easily palpated on clinical examination.

questions.learning_objective: Name the central group as the axillary lymph nodes found in the fat at the base of the axilla.

questions.title: Wall of the axilla where coracobrachialis lies
questions.question: The coracobrachialis muscle lies at which wall of the axilla?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The anterior wall is formed by pectoralis major, pectoralis minor and the clavipectoral fascia.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The posterior wall is formed by subscapularis, teres major and latissimus dorsi.
explanations.C: Correct. The lateral wall of the axilla is the narrow bony/muscular strip formed by the humerus (bicipital groove) together with coracobrachialis and the short head of biceps — this is also the wall along which the axillary vessels and brachial plexus cords run, closer to the anterior than the posterior wall. Coracobrachialis and the short head of biceps together with the humeral bicipital groove make up this narrow lateral wall, distinct from the broader anterior, posterior and medial walls.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The medial wall is formed by serratus anterior overlying the upper ribs.

questions.learning_objective: State that coracobrachialis (with the humerus and short head of biceps) forms the lateral wall of the axilla.

questions.title: Root value of the medial cord of the brachial plexus
questions.question: The medial cord of the brachial plexus originates from:

explanations.A: Incorrect. C5, 6, 7 (the upper and middle trunks' anterior divisions) form the lateral cord, not the medial cord.
explanations.B: Incorrect. C5, 6 alone form the upper trunk, not a cord.
explanations.C: Incorrect. C7 alone (the middle trunk's posterior division, combined with the other two posterior divisions) contributes to the posterior cord, not the medial cord on its own.
explanations.D: Correct. The medial cord is formed from the anterior division of the lower trunk alone, which carries C8 and T1 fibres — the same two roots that make the ulnar nerve (the medial cord's direct continuation) and the medial contribution to the median nerve almost entirely lower-plexus in origin. Because it draws on only the lowest two roots, the medial cord and everything it goes on to form (chiefly the ulnar nerve) carries none of the upper-plexus C5 fibres that the lateral and posterior cords share.

questions.learning_objective: State that the medial cord of the brachial plexus carries C8 and T1 fibres.

questions.title: The one branch given off from a trunk of the brachial plexus
questions.question: ... is a branch from a trunk of the brachial plexus.

explanations.A: Incorrect. The axillary nerve is a terminal branch of the posterior cord, not a trunk branch.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The long thoracic nerve arises directly from the roots (C5-C7), before the trunks even form.
explanations.C: Correct. The nerve to subclavius is the brachial plexus's only true trunk-level branch, arising from the upper trunk (C5, C6) and running down in front of the plexus to reach subclavius. Every other named branch arises either from a root (long thoracic, dorsal scapular) or from a cord (the five terminal branches and their preceding cord-level branches), which is exactly why this single trunk branch is worth remembering as the exception.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The dorsal scapular nerve arises directly from the C5 root, before the trunks form.

questions.learning_objective: Name the nerve to subclavius as the brachial plexus's one true trunk-level branch.

questions.title: Part of the brachial plexus receiving C8 contributions
questions.question: The following part or branch of the brachial plexus receives contributions from the C8 spinal nerve:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The lateral cord is formed from the anterior divisions of the upper and middle trunks (C5-C7), with no C8 contribution.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The lateral pectoral nerve arises from the lateral cord (C5-C7), with no C8 contribution.
explanations.C: Correct. The posterior cord is formed from the posterior divisions of all three trunks — upper, middle and lower — so it draws on the full C5-T1 range, including C8 (via the lower trunk's posterior division). This is the only cord that receives a contribution from every one of the five roots.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The nerve to subclavius arises from the upper trunk (C5, C6), with no C8 contribution.

questions.learning_objective: State that the posterior cord is the only cord receiving a contribution from all five roots, C5 through T1.

questions.title: Exception among branches of the posterior cord
questions.question: The following are branches of the posterior cord of the brachial plexus EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect (true, not the exception). The radial nerve is the posterior cord's largest terminal branch.
explanations.B: Incorrect (true, not the exception). The thoracodorsal nerve, supplying latissimus dorsi, arises from the posterior cord.
explanations.C: Correct. The long thoracic nerve arises directly from the roots (C5-C7), well before the cords form — it never touches the posterior cord at all, despite both nerves running in the same general posterior-wall region of the axilla, which is the source of confusion this item exploits. Its superficial course over serratus anterior, rather than a cord-level origin, is exactly why it is grouped with the axillary nerve's neighbours in exam questions despite being anatomically unrelated to any cord.
explanations.D: Incorrect (true, not the exception). The lower subscapular nerve, supplying part of subscapularis and all of teres major, arises from the posterior cord.

questions.learning_objective: Identify the long thoracic nerve as a root-level branch, not a posterior cord branch.

questions.title: Exception among facts about the medial cord
questions.question: Concerning the medial cord of the brachial plexus, all are correct EXCEPT:

options.A: Gives origin to the ulnar nerve
options.B: Forms part of the median nerve
options.C: Contains fibres of the fifth cervical nerve
options.D: Gives a branch to pectoralis minor muscle

explanations.A: Incorrect (true, not the exception). The ulnar nerve is the direct continuation of the medial cord.
explanations.B: Incorrect (true, not the exception). The medial cord contributes the medial root of the median nerve.
explanations.C: Correct. The medial cord is formed purely from C8 and T1 fibres (the lower trunk's anterior division) — it contains no fifth cervical nerve fibres at all. C5 fibres travel instead in the upper trunk and, ultimately, the lateral and posterior cords, never the medial cord.
explanations.D: Incorrect (true, not the exception). The medial pectoral nerve, a branch of the medial cord, supplies pectoralis minor (and part of pectoralis major).

questions.learning_objective: Identify that the medial cord carries only C8/T1 fibres, with no C5 contribution.

questions.title: Root value of the middle trunk of the brachial plexus
questions.question: The middle trunk of the brachial plexus originates from:

explanations.A: Incorrect. C5, 6, 7 together describe the lateral cord's full root value after the trunks recombine, not the middle trunk alone.
explanations.B: Incorrect. C5, 6 form the upper trunk, not the middle trunk.
explanations.C: Correct. The middle trunk is formed from the C7 root alone, continuing unchanged from the root — the only trunk made from a single root rather than two combining, which is why it is sometimes described as simply "C7 continued". Because the middle trunk carries no other root's fibres, C7 dominates the middle trunk's own divisions before they recombine with the upper and lower trunks' divisions in the cords.
explanations.D: Incorrect. C8 + T1 form the lower trunk, not the middle trunk.

questions.learning_objective: State that the middle trunk of the brachial plexus is formed from C7 alone.

questions.title: Cord of origin of the axillary nerve
questions.question: The axillary nerve is a direct branch from ... of the brachial plexus.

explanations.A: Incorrect. The upper trunk gives the nerve to subclavius and the suprascapular nerve, not the axillary nerve.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The lower roots (C8, T1) feed the medial cord and ultimately the ulnar nerve, not the axillary nerve.
explanations.C: Correct. The axillary nerve, together with the radial nerve, is one of the posterior cord's two terminal branches. It leaves the cord in the axilla and passes through the quadrangular space to reach deltoid and teres minor, carrying C5, C6 fibres.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The lateral cord's terminal branches are the musculocutaneous nerve and the lateral root of the median nerve, not the axillary nerve.

questions.learning_objective: State that the axillary nerve is one of the posterior cord's two terminal branches.

questions.title: Counting the parts of the brachial plexus
questions.question: The brachial plexus has:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The brachial plexus has 5 roots (the anterior rami of C5-T1), not 8.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The brachial plexus has 3 trunks (upper, middle, lower), not 5.
explanations.C: Correct. Each of the 3 trunks splits into an anterior and a posterior division, giving 6 divisions in total — 3 anterior (which recombine into the lateral and medial cords) and 3 posterior (which combine into the posterior cord). This is the one count among the four options that is actually correct for the standard 5-roots/3-trunks/6-divisions/3-cords/5-branches sequence.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The brachial plexus has 3 cords (lateral, medial, posterior), not 4.

questions.learning_objective: State the standard 5-roots/3-trunks/6-divisions/3-cords sequence of the brachial plexus and identify that it has 6 divisions.

questions.title: True statement about the brachial plexus
questions.question: Regarding the brachial plexus:

options.A: The divisions lie in the axilla
options.B: The solitary branch from the trunk is the dorsal scapular nerve
options.C: The axillary nerve supplies only one muscle
options.D: The median nerve arises from 2 cords

explanations.A: Incorrect. The divisions lie behind the clavicle, not in the axilla — only the cords and their branches are found in the axilla.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The solitary trunk branch is the nerve to subclavius; the dorsal scapular nerve is a root branch instead.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The axillary nerve supplies two muscles, deltoid and teres minor, plus sensory branches to the shoulder joint and the "regimental badge" skin area.
explanations.D: Correct. The median nerve is formed by two roots that converge in front of (or around) the axillary artery: a lateral root from the lateral cord (C5-C7 fibres) and a medial root from the medial cord (C8, T1 fibres). This dual-cord origin explains why the median nerve carries the full C5-T1 range and why a lesion of either cord alone can produce a partial median nerve deficit.

questions.learning_objective: State that the median nerve is formed by two roots, one from the lateral cord and one from the medial cord.

questions.title: A branch of the posterior cord
questions.question: Which of the following is a branch of the posterior cord of the brachial plexus?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The dorsal scapular nerve arises from the C5 root, before the cords form.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The long thoracic nerve arises from the roots (C5-C7), before the cords form.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The musculocutaneous nerve is a terminal branch of the lateral cord.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The ulnar nerve is the direct continuation of the medial cord.
explanations.E: Correct. The thoracodorsal (middle subscapular) nerve arises from the posterior cord, between the upper and lower subscapular nerves, and supplies latissimus dorsi. All three subscapular-region nerves (upper subscapular, thoracodorsal, lower subscapular) come off the posterior cord as it runs behind the axillary artery, before it terminates as the axillary and radial nerves.

questions.learning_objective: Name the thoracodorsal nerve as a branch of the posterior cord, supplying latissimus dorsi.

questions.title: Nerve injured with a fractured medial epicondyle
questions.question: The nerve most likely to be injured in a fracture of the medial epicondyle is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The radial nerve runs in the spiral groove of the humeral shaft, far from the medial epicondyle.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The axillary nerve is related to the surgical neck of the humerus, not the elbow.
explanations.C: Correct. The ulnar nerve runs in a groove directly behind the medial epicondyle (the "funny bone" location), making it the structure most exposed to a fracture at this exact site — this is one of the most reliable nerve-injury-by-fracture-site correlations in the whole upper limb. This groove is subcutaneous and unprotected by muscle for a short stretch, which is also why compressing the elbow against a hard surface can produce the same tingling sensation without any fracture at all.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The median nerve runs anterior to the elbow, in the cubital fossa, not behind the medial epicondyle.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The musculocutaneous nerve has already ended as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm well above the elbow.

questions.learning_objective: State that the ulnar nerve is at risk with a fracture of the medial epicondyle.

questions.title: Nerve piercing the lateral intermuscular septum
questions.question: Which of the following nerves pierces the lateral intermuscular septum?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The ulnar nerve pierces the medial intermuscular septum, not the lateral one, on its way to the back of the medial epicondyle.
explanations.B: Correct. The radial nerve, after running in the spiral groove on the back of the humerus, pierces the lateral intermuscular septum about two-thirds of the way down the arm to re-enter the anterior compartment, continuing between brachialis and brachioradialis toward the front of the elbow. This lateral-to-medial then medial-to-lateral crossing pattern (radial nerve moving posterior then back to anterior) is a common source of confusion with the ulnar nerve's simpler single medial-septum crossing.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The median nerve runs down the arm in the anterior compartment throughout, crossing the brachial artery but never piercing either intermuscular septum.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The musculocutaneous nerve stays within the anterior compartment, ending as a cutaneous nerve lateral to the biceps tendon, without piercing the lateral septum.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The axillary nerve leaves the axilla via the quadrangular space, well proximal to either intermuscular septum of the arm.

questions.learning_objective: State that the radial nerve pierces the lateral intermuscular septum to re-enter the anterior compartment of the arm.

questions.title: Nerve injury causing sensory loss over the lower deltoid
questions.question: Loss of sensation of the skin over the lower half of deltoid is due to injury of:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The ulnar nerve supplies the skin of the medial hand and one and a half fingers, not the shoulder region.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The radial nerve's cutaneous branches supply the back of the arm and forearm and part of the hand, not the deltoid region specifically.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The median nerve is almost entirely a forearm-and-hand nerve, with no cutaneous supply near the shoulder.
explanations.D: Correct. The axillary nerve's upper lateral cutaneous nerve of the arm supplies the skin over the lower half of deltoid — the classic "regimental badge" area, named for where a badge sits on a uniform sleeve. Testing sensation here is the standard bedside check for axillary nerve integrity after a shoulder dislocation or surgical-neck fracture.

questions.learning_objective: State that axillary nerve injury causes sensory loss over the lower half of deltoid (the "regimental badge" area).

questions.title: Radial nerve branch arising in the axilla
questions.question: Which of the following branches of the radial nerve arises in the axilla?

options.A: Posterior cutaneous nerve of the arm
options.B: Lower lateral cutaneous nerve of the arm

explanations.A: Correct. The posterior cutaneous nerve of the arm is given off by the radial nerve while it is still in the axilla, before the nerve winds around the humeral shaft in the spiral groove — making it the one branch on this list that arises proximal to (not within or beyond) the arm's spiral-groove course. Every other radial nerve branch listed here arises later, either in the spiral groove itself or near the elbow, after the nerve has already left the axilla behind.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The lower lateral cutaneous nerve of the arm arises in the arm itself, after the nerve has entered the spiral groove.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The muscular branch to brachioradialis arises after the radial nerve has pierced the lateral intermuscular septum, near the elbow.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The muscular branch to anconeus arises in the spiral groove, in the arm, not in the axilla.

questions.learning_objective: Name the posterior cutaneous nerve of the arm as the radial nerve branch given off while still in the axilla.

questions.title: Origin of the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm
questions.question: The lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm is a continuation of:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The radial nerve's own cutaneous territory in the forearm is the posterior cutaneous nerve of the forearm, a separate branch.
explanations.B: Correct. After the musculocutaneous nerve has supplied biceps brachii, brachialis and coracobrachialis, it pierces the deep fascia lateral to the biceps tendon at the elbow and continues on as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm — its purely sensory terminal continuation, supplying the skin of the lateral forearm. This transition from a purely motor nerve to a purely sensory one at a single fixed point (lateral to the biceps tendon) is a useful landmark for locating the musculocutaneous nerve's terminal course on cross-section or dissection.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The axillary nerve's cutaneous territory is the shoulder (regimental badge area), not the forearm.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The median nerve has no lateral forearm cutaneous branch; its palmar cutaneous branch supplies the palm, not the forearm.

questions.learning_objective: State that the musculocutaneous nerve continues as the lateral cutaneous nerve of the forearm.

questions.title: Exception among the contents of the cubital fossa
questions.question: The following structures are present in the cubital fossa, EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect (true, not the exception). The median nerve is the most medial content of the cubital fossa.
explanations.B: Correct. The superior ulnar collateral artery leaves the brachial artery higher up in the arm and runs down behind the medial epicondyle with the ulnar nerve — it does not pass through the cubital fossa itself. The fossa's true contents, from lateral to medial, are the biceps tendon, the brachial artery (dividing into radial and ulnar arteries at its apex) and the median nerve, plus the radial nerve tucked at its lateral boundary.
explanations.C: Incorrect (true, not the exception). The brachial artery bifurcates into the radial and ulnar arteries within the cubital fossa.
explanations.D: Incorrect (true, not the exception). The biceps tendon is the most lateral content of the cubital fossa, before it inserts on the radial tuberosity.

questions.learning_objective: Identify that the superior ulnar collateral artery runs behind the medial epicondyle, not through the cubital fossa.

questions.title: Origin of the axillary nerve from the brachial plexus, second version
questions.question: What is the origin of the axillary nerve from the brachial plexus?

explanations.A: Incorrect. No terminal branch arises directly from a trunk; the axillary nerve is a cord-level branch.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The medial cord's terminal branches are the ulnar nerve and the medial root of the median nerve.
explanations.C: Correct. The axillary nerve is one of the posterior cord's two terminal branches (with the radial nerve), carrying C5, C6 fibres to deltoid, teres minor and the shoulder joint capsule. Both terminal branches of the posterior cord — axillary and radial — leave the cord within the axilla itself, though the axillary nerve exits earlier, via the quadrangular space, while the radial nerve continues on into the arm.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The lateral cord's terminal branches are the musculocutaneous nerve and the lateral root of the median nerve.

questions.learning_objective: State that the axillary nerve arises from the posterior cord of the brachial plexus.

questions.title: Position of the median nerve relative to the brachial artery leaving the axilla
questions.question: As it emerges from the axilla, the median nerve lies where with regard to the brachial artery?

explanations.A: Correct. At the point where the median nerve and brachial artery leave the axilla to enter the arm, the nerve lies lateral to the artery — the two structures then cross each other diagonally down the arm, so that by the elbow the nerve has moved to lie medial to the artery, in the cubital fossa. This crossing relation is a frequently tested spatial fact.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The nerve does not lie posterior to the artery at this level; it lies lateral to it.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Medial is the relation at the elbow, after the crossing, not as the pair leaves the axilla.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The nerve does not lie anterior to the artery at this level; it lies lateral to it.

questions.learning_objective: State that the median nerve lies lateral to the brachial artery as it leaves the axilla, crossing to lie medial to it by the elbow.

questions.title: Root value of the ulnar nerve
questions.question: What are the roots of the ulnar nerve?

explanations.A: Incorrect. C5, 6 form the upper trunk and, ultimately, part of the musculocutaneous and axillary nerves, not the ulnar nerve.
explanations.B: Incorrect. C5, 6, 7 describes the lateral cord/musculocutaneous nerve's root value, not the ulnar nerve's.
explanations.C: Correct. The ulnar nerve is the direct continuation of the medial cord, carrying only C8 and T1 fibres — the same two roots as the medial cord itself, since the ulnar nerve receives no separate contribution beyond what the cord already carries. No other nerve in the upper limb has quite so narrow a root value, which is why testing ulnar-nerve-supplied muscles is such a precise way to assess C8/T1 root function in isolation.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Adding C7 is a common error, confusing the ulnar nerve's root value with the median nerve's broader C5-T1 range.

questions.learning_objective: State that the ulnar nerve carries only C8 and T1 fibres.

questions.title: Lateral border of the cubital fossa
questions.question: The lateral border of the cubital fossa is formed by which muscle?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Extensor carpi ulnaris is a posterior-compartment forearm muscle, unrelated to the cubital fossa's borders.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Flexor carpi radialis is a superficial anterior forearm muscle, not one of the fossa's two muscular borders.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Pronator teres forms the medial border of the cubital fossa, not the lateral one.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Brachialis forms the floor of the cubital fossa (with supinator), not its lateral border.
explanations.E: Correct. The cubital fossa is a triangular hollow whose lateral border is formed by brachioradialis and whose medial border is formed by pronator teres, with an imaginary line between the humeral epicondyles as its base. Brachioradialis, arising from the lateral supracondylar ridge, is the muscle a student would trace along the lateral edge of this triangle.

questions.learning_objective: Name brachioradialis as forming the lateral border of the cubital fossa, and pronator teres as forming the medial border.

questions.title: Nerve supply of biceps brachii
questions.question: The nerve supply of biceps brachii muscle is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The median nerve runs through the arm without supplying any of its anterior compartment muscles.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The ulnar nerve, likewise, runs through the arm without supplying arm muscles; its motor territory begins in the forearm.
explanations.C: Correct. The musculocutaneous nerve is the motor nerve of the whole anterior (flexor) compartment of the arm — biceps brachii, brachialis and coracobrachialis — reflecting its name ("musculo-" for the muscles it supplies on the way, "-cutaneous" for the skin nerve it becomes afterward). Its name itself is a mnemonic for this dual role — "musculo-" for the three muscles it supplies in the arm, "-cutaneous" for the sensory nerve it becomes afterward in the forearm.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The radial nerve supplies the posterior (extensor) compartment of the arm (triceps, anconeus) plus a small lateral strip of brachialis, not biceps brachii.

questions.learning_objective: State that the musculocutaneous nerve supplies biceps brachii.

questions.title: The main flexor of the forearm
questions.question: The main flexor of the forearm is:

explanations.A: Incorrect. Coracobrachialis flexes and adducts the arm at the shoulder joint; it has no forearm action, since it does not cross the elbow.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Subscapularis medially rotates the arm at the shoulder joint and does not act on the elbow at all.
explanations.C: Correct. Brachialis, inserting on the ulnar tuberosity and coronoid process, is the true "workhorse" flexor of the elbow — it flexes the forearm regardless of forearm position (unlike biceps, which flexes best when supinated) and is supplied mainly by the musculocutaneous nerve with a small radial nerve contribution laterally. Biceps, by contrast, is a better-known but functionally secondary flexor, most effective when the forearm is supinated, which is why brachialis rather than biceps is credited as the forearm's principal flexor.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Deltoid abducts, flexes and extends the arm at the shoulder joint, with no action on the forearm at all.

questions.learning_objective: Name brachialis as the main flexor of the forearm at the elbow.

questions.title: Origin of the superior ulnar collateral artery
questions.question: The superior ulnar collateral artery is a direct branch of which artery?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The ulnar artery is downstream of the elbow anastomosis, not the source of the superior ulnar collateral.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The radial artery, likewise, is downstream of the elbow anastomosis.
explanations.C: Correct. The superior ulnar collateral artery arises directly from the brachial artery in the middle of the arm and runs down with the ulnar nerve to the back of the medial epicondyle, anastomosing there with the posterior ulnar recurrent artery — one limb of the rich collateral network around the elbow that keeps the forearm perfused if the brachial artery is compressed or occluded near the joint. This anastomotic link is functionally important because it lets blood reach the forearm around a blockage or compression near the elbow joint, one limb of a larger network fed from both the brachial artery above and the ulnar artery's recurrent branches below.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Profunda brachii arises from the brachial artery higher up and travels with the radial nerve in the spiral groove — a different vessel from the superior ulnar collateral.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The axillary artery has already become the brachial artery well above this level.

questions.learning_objective: State that the superior ulnar collateral artery arises from the brachial artery.

questions.title: Structure behind the medial epicondyle
questions.question: The back of the medial epicondyle is related to the:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The radial nerve is related to the spiral groove of the humeral shaft, not the medial epicondyle.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The axillary nerve is related to the surgical neck of the humerus, far proximal to the elbow.
explanations.C: Correct. The ulnar nerve runs in a palpable groove directly behind the medial epicondyle, before passing between the two heads of flexor carpi ulnaris to enter the forearm — this superficial, exposed position is exactly why a knock to the "funny bone" produces the characteristic tingling down the little and ring fingers. Because the nerve is subcutaneous at exactly this point, it is also the classic site used to elicit Tinel's sign by tapping over the groove.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The median nerve passes in front of the elbow, through the cubital fossa, not behind the medial epicondyle.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The ulnar nerve is indeed related to this site, so "none of the above" is wrong.

questions.learning_objective: State that the ulnar nerve runs behind the medial epicondyle.

questions.title: Structure deep to the bicipital aponeurosis
questions.question: The bicipital aponeurosis lies deep to the:

explanations.A: Incorrect. The bicipital aponeurosis lies superficial to, and protects, the brachial artery — the artery is deep to the aponeurosis, not the reverse relation this option describes.
explanations.B: Correct. The median cubital vein, which links the cephalic and basilic veins across the front of the cubital fossa, lies superficial to the bicipital aponeurosis, so the aponeurosis lies deep to the vein. This layering is exactly what makes venipuncture at the median cubital vein safe — the tough aponeurosis shields the brachial artery and median nerve underneath from a needle that goes slightly too deep.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The median nerve lies deep to the aponeurosis, alongside the brachial artery, not superficial to it.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The radial nerve is not in the cubital fossa's midline at all, let alone superficial to the aponeurosis.
explanations.E: Incorrect. The median cubital vein does lie superficial to the aponeurosis, so "none of the above" is wrong.

questions.learning_objective: State that the median cubital vein lies superficial to the bicipital aponeurosis, which protects the brachial artery and median nerve beneath it.

questions.title: Action of coracobrachialis
questions.question: In movements of the arm, coracobrachialis assists in:

explanations.A: Correct. Coracobrachialis, running from the coracoid process to the middle of the medial humeral shaft, flexes and adducts the arm at the shoulder joint — one of the three muscles supplied by the musculocutaneous nerve, which characteristically pierces it on the way into the arm. This flexor role places coracobrachialis alongside pectoralis major and the anterior fibres of deltoid as the shoulder's principal flexors, even though it is a much smaller muscle than either.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Coracobrachialis flexes, the opposite action to extension.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Coracobrachialis adducts the arm, the opposite action to abduction.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Coracobrachialis has no significant rotator action at the shoulder.
explanations.E: Incorrect. Supination is a forearm movement at the radioulnar joints; coracobrachialis does not cross the elbow or forearm at all.

questions.learning_objective: State that coracobrachialis flexes (and adducts) the arm at the shoulder joint.

questions.title: Part of brachialis supplied by the musculocutaneous nerve
questions.question: The musculocutaneous nerve supplies which part of brachialis?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Brachioradialis is supplied entirely by the radial nerve, not the musculocutaneous nerve, so neither part of it fits this question.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Same reasoning as A — brachioradialis is a radial-nerve muscle throughout.
explanations.C: Correct. Brachialis is unusual in having a dual nerve supply: the musculocutaneous nerve supplies the medial (larger) part, which is purely motor, while the radial nerve supplies a lateral strip that carries some proprioceptive fibres — a detail that explains why brachialis is not simply listed as "purely musculocutaneous" the way biceps and coracobrachialis are. This partial radial nerve supply also explains why an isolated musculocutaneous nerve lesion weakens, but does not completely abolish, elbow flexion via brachialis.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The lateral part of brachialis is the radial nerve's contribution, not the musculocutaneous nerve's.

questions.learning_objective: State that the musculocutaneous nerve supplies the medial part of brachialis, while the radial nerve supplies a lateral strip.

questions.title: Needle site for a brachial artery blood sample
questions.question: You are planning to take a blood sample from the brachial artery. Where should you insert the needle?

options.A: In the lateral aspect of the arm, between biceps and triceps
options.B: Just medial to the biceps tendon in the cubital fossa
options.C: Just lateral to the biceps tendon in the cubital fossa
options.D: Just medial to the tendon of flexor carpi radialis at the wrist

explanations.A: Incorrect. The lateral arm between biceps and triceps does not overlie the brachial artery's most accessible, superficial point.
explanations.B: Correct. In the cubital fossa, the brachial artery lies just medial to the biceps tendon (with the median nerve further medial still) — this landmark ordering, tendon then artery then nerve from lateral to medial, is exactly why "just medial to the biceps tendon" is the safe, reliable needle site for sampling or accessing the brachial artery. This same landmark is used whether the goal is drawing a blood sample, inserting an arterial line, or simply palpating the pulse before either procedure.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Just lateral to the biceps tendon overlies the tendon itself and the radial nerve's approach, not the artery.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Medial to flexor carpi radialis at the wrist is the landmark for the radial artery, not the brachial artery.

questions.learning_objective: State that the brachial artery lies just medial to the biceps tendon in the cubital fossa, the standard landmark for sampling it.

questions.title: Exception among branches of the radial nerve
questions.question: Which of the following is NOT a branch of the radial nerve?

options.A: Posterior cutaneous nerve of the arm
options.B: Upper lateral cutaneous nerve of the arm
options.C: Posterior cutaneous nerve of the forearm
options.D: Lower lateral cutaneous nerve of the arm

explanations.A: Incorrect (true, not the exception). The posterior cutaneous nerve of the arm is given off by the radial nerve while still in the axilla.
explanations.B: Correct. The upper lateral cutaneous nerve of the arm is actually a branch of the axillary nerve, not the radial nerve — it supplies the "regimental badge" skin over the lower deltoid. Its similar name to the radial nerve's own lower lateral cutaneous nerve of the arm is exactly the trap this item sets.
explanations.C: Incorrect (true, not the exception). The posterior cutaneous nerve of the forearm is given off in the spiral groove, supplying the skin over the back of the forearm.
explanations.D: Incorrect (true, not the exception). The lower lateral cutaneous nerve of the arm is a genuine radial nerve branch, given off in the spiral groove.

questions.learning_objective: Identify that the upper lateral cutaneous nerve of the arm belongs to the axillary nerve, not the radial nerve.

questions.title: Exception among muscles supplied by the radial nerve
questions.question: All of these muscles are supplied by the radial nerve EXCEPT:

explanations.A: Incorrect (true, not the exception). Brachioradialis is entirely radial-nerve supplied, despite being functionally a flexor.
explanations.B: Incorrect (true, not the exception). Extensor carpi radialis longus is one of the radial nerve's forearm extensor muscles.
explanations.C: Incorrect (true, not the exception). The lateral head of triceps, like all three heads, is supplied by the radial nerve.
explanations.D: Correct. Coracobrachialis is supplied purely by the musculocutaneous nerve, with no radial nerve contribution at all — unlike its neighbour brachialis, which does receive a small radial nerve branch to its lateral part, making coracobrachialis the cleaner, unambiguous exception among these five muscles. This distinction — coracobrachialis with no radial contribution at all, versus brachialis with a genuine (if partial) one — is precisely the kind of detail this EXCEPT-style question is designed to test.
explanations.E: Incorrect (true, not the exception). Brachialis does receive a radial nerve contribution to its lateral part, alongside its main musculocutaneous supply.

questions.learning_objective: Identify coracobrachialis as the one muscle in this list with no radial nerve supply at all.

questions.title: Structure damaged by a stab wound to the medial cubital fossa
questions.question: A 35-year-old man has a stab wound to the most medial side of the cubital fossa. Which of the following structures would most likely be damaged?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The biceps tendon is the most lateral, not medial, content of the cubital fossa.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The radial nerve lies at the fossa's lateral boundary, tucked between brachioradialis and brachialis, not medially.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The brachial artery lies just medial to the biceps tendon, in the middle of the fossa, not at its most medial edge.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The radial recurrent artery arises further down, in the forearm proper, not at the medial edge of the cubital fossa.
explanations.E: Correct. From lateral to medial, the cubital fossa's contents run: biceps tendon, brachial artery, median nerve — making the median nerve the single most medial structure at this level, and therefore the one most exposed to a stab wound entering from the medial side. A stab wound entering from the medial side therefore threatens the nerve well before it reaches the artery or the tendon, which lie further lateral.

questions.learning_objective: State that the median nerve is the most medial content of the cubital fossa.

questions.title: Muscle weakened by a lateral cord lesion
questions.question: A 20-year-old man fell and was diagnosed with a lesion of the lateral cord of the brachial plexus. Which of the following muscles is most likely weakened by this injury?

explanations.A: Incorrect. Subscapularis is supplied by the upper and lower subscapular nerves, both posterior cord branches.
explanations.B: Incorrect. Teres major is supplied by the lower subscapular nerve, a posterior cord branch.
explanations.C: Incorrect. Latissimus dorsi is supplied by the thoracodorsal nerve, a posterior cord branch.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Teres minor is supplied by the axillary nerve, a posterior cord branch.
explanations.E: Correct. The lateral pectoral nerve, a branch of the lateral cord, supplies the clavicular head of pectoralis major (the sternocostal head is supplied by the medial pectoral nerve from the medial cord instead). Since all four other options are posterior cord muscles, pectoralis major is the only one on this list actually weakened by a lateral cord lesion.

questions.learning_objective: Reason that the lateral pectoral nerve (from the lateral cord) supplies the clavicular head of pectoralis major, distinguishing it from the four posterior-cord-supplied distractors.

questions.title: Structures injured with a midshaft humeral fracture
questions.question: In case of a midshaft fracture of the humerus, which pair of structures could most likely be injured at the fracture site?

options.A: Radial nerve and deep brachial artery
options.B: Axillary nerve and posterior humeral circumflex artery
options.C: Long thoracic nerve and lateral thoracic artery

explanations.A: Correct. The radial nerve and the profunda brachii (deep brachial) artery travel together in the spiral groove on the posterior surface of the humeral shaft, exactly at the level of a midshaft fracture — making this the classic paired injury taught with humeral shaft fractures, distinct from the axillary-nerve/surgical-neck pairing. This same spiral-groove relation is also why radial nerve palsy (wrist drop) is a well-recognised complication specifically of midshaft, rather than proximal or distal, humeral fractures.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral artery are related to the surgical neck of the humerus, proximal to the midshaft.
explanations.C: Incorrect. The long thoracic nerve and lateral thoracic artery run on serratus anterior's surface on the chest wall, unrelated to the humeral shaft.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The suprascapular nerve and artery are related to the scapula (suprascapular notch), not the humeral shaft.

questions.learning_objective: State that the radial nerve and profunda brachii artery are the pair at risk in a humeral midshaft fracture.

questions.title: Needle site for arterial blood gas sampling from the brachial artery
questions.question: A 45-year-old woman has severe bronchial asthma and needs an arterial blood sample from the brachial artery. Where should the technician insert the needle?

options.A: Just medial to the tendon of flexor carpi radialis muscle at the wrist
options.B: In the lateral aspect of the arm, between the biceps and triceps brachii muscles
options.C: Just medial to the biceps tendon in the cubital fossa
options.D: Just lateral to the biceps tendon in the cubital fossa

explanations.A: Incorrect. This landmark, medial to flexor carpi radialis at the wrist, locates the radial artery, not the brachial artery.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The lateral arm between biceps and triceps is not the recognised access point for the brachial artery.
explanations.C: Correct. As in the earlier venipuncture-style question on this same bank, the brachial artery lies just medial to the biceps tendon in the cubital fossa, the standard, reliable site for accessing it — including for arterial blood gas sampling in a patient with respiratory disease such as this asthma vignette. The same landmark works regardless of the clinical indication, whether arterial blood gas sampling for a respiratory patient or simple pulse palpation.
explanations.D: Incorrect. Just lateral to the biceps tendon overlies the tendon and radial nerve territory, not the artery.

questions.learning_objective: State that the brachial artery is accessed just medial to the biceps tendon in the cubital fossa.

questions.title: Structure most liable to injury in medial cubital fossa surgery
questions.question: During surgical intervention in the medial part of the cubital fossa, which structure is more liable to be injured?

explanations.A: Incorrect. The brachial artery lies more centrally in the fossa, medial to the biceps tendon but lateral to the nerve.
explanations.B: Incorrect. The radial nerve lies at the fossa's lateral boundary, the opposite side from where this question is asking.
explanations.C: Correct. The median nerve is the most medial structure in the cubital fossa, so surgery on the medial side of the fossa places it at greatest risk — the same lateral-to-medial ordering (biceps tendon, brachial artery, median nerve) that makes this the consistent answer whenever a cubital fossa question specifies the medial side. This is why surgeons approaching the cubital fossa from its medial side take particular care to identify and protect the nerve before proceeding, in contrast to a lateral approach where the biceps tendon is the main structure at risk instead.
explanations.D: Incorrect. The biceps tendon is the most lateral content of the fossa, the opposite side from where this question is asking.

questions.learning_objective: State that the median nerve, as the most medial content of the cubital fossa, is most at risk in medial-approach surgery there.
